records.source: ὥστε, ἀδελφοί μου ἀγαπητοὶ καὶ ἐπιπόθητοι, χαρὰ καὶ στέφανός μου, οὕτως στήκετε ἐν κυρίῳ, ἀγαπητοί.
records.gloss: Therefore, brothers of me, beloved and longed for, joy and crown of me, in this way stand firm in [the] Lord, beloved.
pieces: So then, my dear {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, whom I love and long to see, my joy and my crown: stand firm in the Lord in this way, dear friends.

L.1: Therefore, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, in this way stand firm in [the] Lord, beloved.

R.1: So, my dear {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, I love you and miss you. You are my joy and my crown of victory. Keep standing firm in the Lord, as I have shown you, dear friends.

decisions.choice: fellow believers, women and men
decisions.reason: ἀδελφοί addresses the whole church; verse 2 names two women in it.

decisions.choice: the victor's wreath
decisions.reason: στέφανος is the wreath given to a winner or honoured guest, not a king's crown. Paul uses it of the people he will be proud of when Christ returns (compare 1 Thessalonians 2:19).

decisions.choice: in this way: as just described
decisions.reason: οὕτως points back to chapter 3: stand firm by following Paul's example and waiting for the Saviour.

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: Paul is addressing the whole church, which includes the women he names in verse 2, so the inclusive default spells that out. Traditional is one tap away.

decisions.choice: my crown of victory
decisions.reason: Plain English readers hear "crown" as royalty; "of victory" carries the wreath image.

records.heading: Stand firm in the Lord

records.source: Εὐοδίαν παρακαλῶ καὶ Συντύχην παρακαλῶ τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν ἐν κυρίῳ.
records.gloss: Euodia I urge and Syntyche I urge the same to think in [the] Lord.
pieces: I appeal to Euodia and I appeal to Syntyche to agree with each other in the Lord.

L.2: I urge Euodia and I urge Syntyche to think the same thing in [the] Lord.

R.2: I am pleading with Euodia and with Syntyche to agree with each other, as people who belong to the Lord.

decisions.choice: the same appeal, made to each woman separately
decisions.reason: Repeating παρακαλῶ treats the two women evenly; Paul does not take sides. Literal and Balanced keep the repetition.

decisions.choice: to share one mind and attitude
decisions.reason: φρονέω is a key word in this letter (2:2, 2:5): a whole way of thinking, not agreement on every detail.

decisions.choice: two women who led in the church
decisions.reason: Both names are feminine. Verse 3 says they fought side by side with Paul for the gospel, so they were workers in the church, not bystanders.

records.source: ναὶ ἐρωτῶ καὶ σέ, γνήσιε σύζυγε, συλλαμβάνου αὐταῖς, αἵτινες ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ συνήθλησάν μοι μετὰ καὶ Κλήμεντος καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν συνεργῶν μου, ὧν τὰ ὀνόματα ἐν βίβλῳ ζωῆς.
records.gloss: Yes, I ask also you, true yokefellow, help them, who in the gospel contended alongside me with also Clement and the rest of fellow workers of me, whose names [are] in [the] book of life.
pieces: Yes, and I ask you, my true partner, to help these women. They have fought side by side with me for the gospel, together with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.

L.3: Yes, I ask you also, true yokefellow, help them, [women] who contended alongside me in the gospel, together with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names [are] in [the] book of life.

R.3: And you, my loyal partner, please help these women. They worked hard with me to spread the good news, along with Clement and my other co-workers. Their names are written in the book of life.

decisions.choice: a loyal partner, unnamed
decisions.reason: σύζυγε means one yoked together with another. It may be a personal name, and Paul may be punning on it ("truly a Yokefellow"). Who is meant is unknown. A footnote gives the name reading.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT
alternatives: the same two words in the other order
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT marks a variant in the order of these two words. The meaning does not change, so there is no footnote.

decisions.choice: contended side by side, as athletes or soldiers
decisions.reason: συναθλέω is a contest word, used again in 1:27 of striving together for the faith.

decisions.choice: God's register of his people
decisions.reason: The book of life appears in Exodus 32:32, Daniel 12:1 and Revelation 3:5: God's own list of those who belong to him.

decisions.choice: these women / [women]
decisions.reason: The Greek pronouns are feminine; English "them" would hide that the people to be helped are Euodia and Syntyche.

decisions.choice: worked hard with me
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the effort but loses the contest image; the meaning note gives it.

records.source: Χαίρετε ἐν κυρίῳ πάντοτε· πάλιν ἐρῶ, χαίρετε.
records.gloss: Rejoice in [the] Lord always; again I will say, rejoice.
pieces: Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: rejoice!

L.4: Rejoice in [the] Lord always; again I will say, rejoice.

R.4: Always be full of joy in the Lord. I'll say it again: be full of joy!

decisions.choice: a command to rejoice, repeated
alternatives: "farewell", the same word as a goodbye
decisions.reason: Χαίρετε was also an everyday greeting, but "always" and the repetition make it a command here.

decisions.choice: joy whose ground is the Lord
decisions.reason: The joy is located in the Lord, which is why it can be commanded "always", even from prison.

decisions.choice: be full of joy
decisions.reason: "Rejoice" is now mostly church language; Readable says what it means.

records.heading: Rejoice in the Lord always

records.source: τὸ ἐπιεικὲς ὑμῶν γνωσθήτω πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις.
records.gloss: The gentleness of you let be known to all human beings.
pieces: Let your gentleness be evident to {{gender:everyone|all men}}.

L.5: Let your gentleness be known to all {{gender:people|men}}.

R.5: Let {{gender:everyone|all men}} see how gentle and gracious you are.

decisions.choice: gentle graciousness: not insisting on one's rights
decisions.reason: ἐπιεικής has no single equivalent. It describes someone who yields rather than demands, the opposite of a quarrel like the one in verse 2.

decisions.choice: everyone, not only believers
decisions.reason: Generic, so the gender setting applies.

decisions.choice: {{gender:everyone|all men}}
decisions.reason: Inclusive default.

records.source: ὁ κύριος ἐγγύς·
records.gloss: The Lord [is] near.
pieces: The Lord is near.

decisions.choice: near, in both time and presence
decisions.reason: ἐγγύς can mean the Lord's return is near or that he is close to his people now. Paul may mean both; "near" keeps both open.

decisions.choice: echoes Psalm 145:18
decisions.reason: The Greek Psalm says the Lord is near to all who call on him, where "Lord" stands for God's name. Following the charter, the New Testament κύριος is always "Lord"; the note gives the echo.

records.source: μηδὲν μεριμνᾶτε, ἀλλ’ ἐν παντὶ τῇ προσευχῇ καὶ τῇ δεήσει μετ’ εὐχαριστίας τὰ αἰτήματα ὑμῶν γνωριζέσθω πρὸς τὸν θεόν· καὶ ἡ εἰρήνη τοῦ θεοῦ ἡ ὑπερέχουσα πάντα νοῦν φρουρήσει τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν καὶ τὰ νοήματα ὑμῶν ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
records.gloss: Nothing be anxious about, but in everything by the prayer and the petition with thanksgiving the requests of you let be made known to God; \v 7 and the peace of God surpassing every understanding will guard the hearts of you and the thoughts of you in Christ Jesus.
pieces: Do not worry about anything. Instead, in everything, bring your requests to God through prayer and petition, with thanksgiving.
And God's peace, which is beyond all our understanding, will stand guard over your hearts and your minds in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus.

L.6: Be anxious about nothing; rather, in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God;
L.7: and the peace of God, which surpasses every understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus.

R.6: Do not be worried about anything. Whatever happens, talk to God about it. Ask {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for what you need, and thank {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} while you ask.
R.7: And God's peace, which is more than our minds can grasp, will keep watch over your hearts and thoughts, because you are joined to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus.

decisions.choice: do not be anxious about anything
decisions.reason: μεριμνάω is anxious care, the word Jesus uses in Matthew 6:25-34. In 2:20 Paul uses it in a good sense, of Timothy's concern for others; here the context makes it worry.

decisions.choice: prayer in general, and specific requests
decisions.reason: προσευχή is prayer of every kind; δέησις is asking for something particular. Together they mean: bring everything to God, including the specifics.

decisions.choice: thanksgiving goes with the asking
decisions.reason: εὐχαριστίας accompanies the requests; it is not made to wait for the outcome.

decisions.choice: the result: God's peace follows
decisions.reason: The καὶ introduces what follows from bringing everything to God. It is a promise, not a payment for praying well.

decisions.choice: beyond what the mind can grasp
decisions.reason: The phrase can mean God's peace is beyond understanding, or that it achieves more than any human scheming could. Both fit; we follow the more common reading and note the other.

decisions.choice: a military guard
decisions.reason: φρουρέω is what a garrison does. Philippi was a Roman colony with retired soldiers among its citizens, so the image would have been vivid.

decisions.choice: the inner life and its thoughts
decisions.reason: In biblical usage the heart is the centre of the person; νόημα is a thought or plan. Together: the whole inner life.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: stand guard over (B); keep watch over (R)
decisions.reason: Keeps the military image without the archaic "keep".

decisions.choice: because you are joined to
decisions.reason: "In Christ" means being united to him; Readable says so. This adds a reason ("because") that the Greek leaves implicit; reviewers should check it.

records.source: Τὸ λοιπόν, ἀδελφοί, ὅσα ἐστὶν ἀληθῆ, ὅσα σεμνά, ὅσα δίκαια, ὅσα ἁγνά, ὅσα προσφιλῆ, ὅσα εὔφημα, εἴ τις ἀρετὴ καὶ εἴ τις ἔπαινος, ταῦτα λογίζεσθε·
records.gloss: As for the rest, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever honorable, whatever just, whatever pure, whatever lovely, whatever well spoken of, if any virtue and if any praise, these things consider.
pieces: Finally, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}: all that is true, all that is honorable, all that is just, all that is pure, all that is lovely, all that is well spoken of—if there is any virtue, anything that deserves praise—let your minds dwell on these things.

L.8: Finally, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, whatever is true, whatever honorable, whatever right, whatever pure, whatever lovely, whatever well spoken of, if [there is] any virtue and if any praise, consider these things.

R.8: Finally, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, fill your minds with good things: things that are true and honorable, right and pure, lovely and admired by others. Think about whatever is excellent and deserves praise.

decisions.choice: as for the rest: a turn to the final instructions
decisions.reason: λοιπόν marks a transition, not necessarily the last sentence; Paul used it already in 3:1.

decisions.choice: fellow believers, women and men
decisions.reason: As in verse 1.

decisions.choice: virtues any decent person would recognise
decisions.reason: Several words in this list, especially ἀρετὴ (virtue, excellence), belong to the moral vocabulary of Greek philosophy and appear nowhere else in Paul. He commends what is good wherever it is found.

decisions.choice: worthy of respect, dignified
decisions.reason: σεμνός describes what is serious and deserves reverence: dignified rather than trivial.

decisions.choice: well spoken of, of good report
decisions.reason: εὔφημος occurs only here in the New Testament: things people speak well of.

decisions.choice: take into account; dwell on deliberately
decisions.reason: λογίζομαι is a reckoning word: careful, continued consideration that shapes action, which verse 9 then calls for.

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: Paul is addressing the whole church, which includes the women he names in verse 2, so the inclusive default spells that out. Traditional is one tap away.

records.source: ἃ καὶ ἐμάθετε καὶ παρελάβετε καὶ ἠκούσατε καὶ εἴδετε ἐν ἐμοί, ταῦτα πράσσετε· καὶ ὁ θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης ἔσται μεθ’ ὑμῶν.
records.gloss: The things also you learned and received and heard and saw in me, these things practice; and the God of peace will be with you.
pieces: Put into practice what you learned and received from me, what you heard and saw in me. And the God of peace will be with you.

L.9: What you both learned and received and heard and saw in me, practice these things; and the God of peace will be with you.

R.9: Keep doing everything you learned from me, everything I taught you, and everything you heard me say and saw me do. Then the God who gives peace will be with you.

decisions.choice: received as handed-on teaching
decisions.reason: παραλαμβάνω is the word for receiving a tradition passed on by a teacher (1 Corinthians 15:3).

decisions.choice: teaching and example together
decisions.reason: The first two verbs are about what Paul taught; the last two about what they heard and saw of his life.

decisions.choice: the God who is the source of peace
decisions.reason: Verse 7 promised the peace of God; here the God of peace himself will be with them.

decisions.choice: the God who gives peace
decisions.reason: Readable makes the genitive explicit.

records.source: Ἐχάρην δὲ ἐν κυρίῳ μεγάλως ὅτι ἤδη ποτὲ ἀνεθάλετε τὸ ὑπὲρ ἐμοῦ φρονεῖν, ἐφ’ ᾧ καὶ ἐφρονεῖτε ἠκαιρεῖσθε δέ.
records.gloss: I rejoiced and in [the] Lord greatly that now at last you blossomed again the on behalf of me to think, on which also you were thinking, you were lacking opportunity however.
pieces: It brought me great joy in the Lord that now at last your care for me has come into bloom again. You had been caring all along; you simply had no chance to show it.

L.10: And I rejoiced in [the] Lord greatly that now at last you have blossomed again in thinking of me; [you were] indeed thinking [of me], but you lacked opportunity.

R.10: I am so glad in the Lord that your care for me has blossomed again, like a plant that flowers again after a dry season. I know you cared about me the whole time, but you had no chance to show it.

decisions.choice: blossomed again, like a plant putting out new growth
decisions.reason: ἀναθάλλω is used of plants that sprout or flower again. Paul pictures their care for him as a plant coming back into flower after a season without blossom. It is not a rebuke for letting their care die: the end of the verse says they cared all along.

decisions.choice: now at last: after a long gap
alternatives: now finally, after you neglected me
decisions.reason: The words mark a long interval since their last gift. Paul explains the gap at once as a lack of opportunity, not a lack of love.

decisions.choice: you were concerned all along, but had no opportunity
alternatives: you were concerned about the matter, but the time was not right
decisions.reason: The words "for which" point back to their concern for Paul. ἀκαιρέομαι means to lack a fitting time. Paul does not say what stood in the way: distance, a messenger, or their own deep poverty, which 2 Corinthians 8:2 mentions in the churches of Macedonia.

decisions.choice: joy in the Lord, not only in the money
decisions.reason: Paul's joy is "in the Lord", the phrase of 4:4. He was glad because their gift showed the Lord at work in them; verses 11 and 17 make clear he is not rejoicing over the money as such.

decisions.choice: come into bloom again (B); blossomed again, like a plant (R)
decisions.reason: "Revived" loses the picture of a plant flowering again. Readable spells the picture out as a comparison; "after a dry season" adds only what the image itself implies.

decisions.choice: to show it
decisions.reason: The Greek says only that they lacked opportunity. Verses 14-18 show that the opportunity was to act on their care by sending help, so Balanced and Readable add "to show it".

records.heading: Thanks for their gift

records.source: οὐχ ὅτι καθ’ ὑστέρησιν λέγω, ἐγὼ γὰρ ἔμαθον ἐν οἷς εἰμι αὐτάρκης εἶναι·
records.gloss: Not that according to need I speak, I for learned in [the things] in which I am content to be;
pieces: I do not say this because I am going short. However things stand with me, I have learned to be content.

L.11: Not that I speak according to need, for I have learned to be content in whatever [circumstances] I am.

R.11: I am not saying this because I am short of anything. I have learned to be content with what I have, whatever happens to me.

decisions.choice: not because I am in want
alternatives: not as a complaint about poverty
decisions.reason: Paul makes sure his thanks are not taken as a hint that he needs more. This is the first of two such disclaimers; the second is in verse 17.

decisions.choice: content: having enough, not ruled by circumstances
decisions.reason: αὐτάρκης was a favorite word of Stoic and Cynic teachers for the wise person who needs nothing outside himself. Paul uses the word but not the idea of self-reliance: verse 13 says his strength comes from the one who strengthens him. He means having enough, whatever he has.

decisions.choice: learned through experience
decisions.reason: The contentment was not a natural temperament. Paul learned it through the hardships he lists in 2 Corinthians 11:23-27.

decisions.choice: in whatever circumstances I am in
alternatives: among whatever people I am with
decisions.reason: The pronoun could refer to people or to things. Verse 12, with its plenty and want, shows Paul means his circumstances.

decisions.choice: content
decisions.reason: "Self-sufficient" suggests not needing anyone, the opposite of verse 13. "Content" says having enough. Readable adds "with what I have" to make that plain.

decisions.choice: going short
decisions.reason: ὑστέρησις is lack or shortage; "going short" says it in everyday words.

records.source: οἶδα καὶ ταπεινοῦσθαι, οἶδα καὶ περισσεύειν· ἐν παντὶ καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν μεμύημαι, καὶ χορτάζεσθαι καὶ πεινᾶν, καὶ περισσεύειν καὶ ὑστερεῖσθαι·
records.gloss: I know also to be brought low, I know also to abound; in every and in all I have been initiated, both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to lack;
pieces: I know how to get by on little, and I know how to handle having plenty. In each and every situation I have been let into the secret: how to eat my fill and how to go hungry, how to have more than enough and how to do without.

L.12: I know both [how] to be brought low, [and] I know [how] to abound; in everything and in all [things] I have been initiated, both into being filled and into being hungry, both into abounding and into lacking.

R.12: I know how to live with very little, and I know how to live with a lot. I have learned the secret of living in every kind of situation: when I have plenty to eat and when I am hungry, when I have more than I need and when I do not have enough.

decisions.choice: to be brought low: to live with little
decisions.reason: The word is paired with "to abound", so it is about circumstances, having little, rather than the humble mind Paul commends in 2:3. The same verb is used of Christ in 2:8, who humbled himself.

decisions.choice: I have been initiated: let into a secret
decisions.reason: μυέομαι was the word for being initiated into the secret rites of the mystery cults, well known in the Greek world. Paul uses it only here. It suggests a secret that is learned by being brought through experience. Verse 13 gives the secret.

decisions.choice: in each and every situation
alternatives: in everything and among all people
decisions.reason: Paul uses the same word in the singular and then the plural. The plural could mean "among all people", but the list that follows is about circumstances, so the doubling stresses that no situation is left out.

decisions.choice: two pairs of opposites
decisions.reason: Full and hungry, plenty and lack: Paul names the extremes to say he has been through both, and both are hard to handle well.

decisions.choice: I have been initiated (L); I have been let into the secret (B)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the picture of being initiated rather than an ordinary word for learning. Readable uses plain words; the meaning note gives the image.

decisions.choice: get by on little ... handle having plenty (B); live with very little ... with a lot (R)
decisions.reason: Says in everyday words what the two verbs mean in this context.

records.source: πάντα ἰσχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με.
records.gloss: All things I have strength for in the [one] strengthening me.
pieces: I have strength for every situation in the one who makes me strong.

L.13: I have strength for all things in the [one who] strengthens me.

R.13: I can face all of it, whether I have plenty or very little, in the strength of the one who makes me strong.

decisions.choice: all things: every circumstance just described
alternatives: anything at all I set out to do
decisions.reason: The sentence completes verses 11-12. "All things" are the conditions Paul has just listed: eating well and going hungry, having plenty and going without. He is saying he can live through any of them and stay content, not that he has unlimited ability. Lifted out of its setting the verse is often heard as a promise of success in any task; the context does not support that.

decisions.choice: have strength for, be equal to
decisions.reason: ἰσχύω means to be strong or capable. With an object it means to be strong enough for something, to cope with it.

decisions.choice: in the one who strengthens me: strength that comes from being joined to him
alternatives: by means of the one who strengthens me
decisions.reason: The preposition can mean "in" or "by". Either way the strength is not Paul's own. Where Stoic teachers spoke of a self-sufficient person (verse 11), Paul's sufficiency comes from someone else.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "the one who strengthens me"
decisions.reason: The oldest manuscripts have no name here; many later ones, followed by the King James Version, add "Christ". The added word names the one Paul almost certainly means: in 1 Timothy 1:12 Christ Jesus strengthens Paul with the same verb, ἐνδυναμόω. So the meaning hardly changes.

decisions.choice: every situation (B); all of it, whether I have plenty or very little (R)
decisions.reason: "All things" on its own is easily heard as a promise of unlimited ability. Balanced says what the context shows "all things" means, and Readable repeats the contrast from verse 12. Literal keeps "all things". Reviewers should check whether Balanced should keep the wider "all things" and leave the context to the note.

records.source: πλὴν καλῶς ἐποιήσατε συγκοινωνήσαντές μου τῇ θλίψει.
records.gloss: Nevertheless well you did having shared together of me the affliction.
pieces: All the same, you did a fine thing when you took a share in my hardship.

L.14: Nevertheless, you did well, sharing together in my affliction.

R.14: Even so, you did the right thing when you shared my hard times with me.

decisions.choice: nevertheless: do not take my contentment as ingratitude
decisions.reason: Having said he can manage with little, Paul makes sure they do not think their gift was unwelcome or unneeded.

decisions.choice: became partners in my hardship
decisions.reason: συγκοινωνέω means to take a share in something together with someone. It belongs to the partnership words that run through the letter (1:5, 1:7). By sending help the Philippians joined in Paul's hardship; they did not only feel sorry for him.

decisions.choice: hardship, distress: here his imprisonment
alternatives: the troubles of the last days
decisions.reason: θλῖψις is pressure or distress of any kind. In this letter it is Paul's imprisonment and its hardships (1:17).

decisions.choice: took a share in
decisions.reason: Keeps the idea of becoming a partner, which verses 15-16 develop.

records.source: Οἴδατε δὲ καὶ ὑμεῖς, Φιλιππήσιοι, ὅτι ἐν ἀρχῇ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου, ὅτε ἐξῆλθον ἀπὸ Μακεδονίας, οὐδεμία μοι ἐκκλησία ἐκοινώνησεν εἰς λόγον δόσεως καὶ λήμψεως εἰ μὴ ὑμεῖς μόνοι, ὅτι καὶ ἐν Θεσσαλονίκῃ καὶ ἅπαξ καὶ δὶς εἰς τὴν χρείαν μοι ἐπέμψατε.
records.gloss: Know and also you, Philippians, that in [the] beginning of the gospel, when I went out from Macedonia, not one to me church shared in [an] account of giving and receiving except you alone, \v 16 that even in Thessalonica both once and twice for the need to me you sent.
pieces: You know it yourselves, Philippians: in those first days of the gospel, when I left Macedonia, yours was the only church that went into partnership with me in an account of giving and receiving.
Even in Thessalonica you sent help for my needs more than once.

L.15: And you yourselves also know, Philippians, that in [the] beginning of the gospel, when I went out from Macedonia, not one church shared with me in [an] account of giving and receiving except you alone;
L.16: for even in Thessalonica you sent [help] to me for [my] need both once and twice.

R.15: You Philippians know this yourselves. In the early days, when you had just heard the good news and I left Macedonia, your church was the only one that became my partner, giving and receiving.
R.16: Even while I was still in Thessalonica, you sent me help more than once when I needed it.

decisions.choice: the beginning of the gospel among them
alternatives: the beginning of the gospel everywhere
decisions.reason: Paul had been preaching for years before he came to Philippi (Galatians 1:17-2:1), so he means the start of the gospel in their region: his first visit to Macedonia, told in Acts 16.

decisions.choice: a shared account of giving and receiving
alternatives: in the matter of giving and receiving
decisions.reason: λόγος here is a bookkeeping word, an account, and "giving and receiving" was a common business phrase for payments made and received. Paul describes their gifts as a partnership with two sides: they gave him material help, and they received from him the gospel (compare Romans 15:27 and 1 Corinthians 9:11).

decisions.choice: the time when Paul moved on from Macedonia
decisions.reason: Acts 16-18 tells how Paul went from Philippi to Thessalonica and Berea, all in Macedonia, and then on to Athens and Corinth. The gifts to Thessalonica (verse 16) came while he was still in Macedonia, and 2 Corinthians 11:9 mentions help from Macedonia when he was in Corinth.

decisions.choice: more than once
decisions.reason: "Both once and twice" is an expression for repeated action; Paul uses the same phrase in 1 Thessalonians 2:18.

decisions.choice: went into partnership
decisions.reason: κοινωνέω is the verb of the partnership Paul thanks them for in 1:5: a commitment, not a single gift.

decisions.choice: [help], [my]
decisions.reason: The Greek has no object for "you sent"; Literal supplies the obvious one in brackets.

decisions.choice: when you had just heard the good news
alternatives: in the beginning of the good news
decisions.reason: Readable spells out what "the beginning of the gospel" means here (meaning note m1).

records.source: οὐχ ὅτι ἐπιζητῶ τὸ δόμα, ἀλλὰ ἐπιζητῶ τὸν καρπὸν τὸν πλεονάζοντα εἰς λόγον ὑμῶν.
records.gloss: Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the fruit the increasing to account of you.
pieces: It is not the gift I am after. What I am after is the profit that keeps adding up in your account.

L.17: Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the fruit that increases to your account.

R.17: I am not hinting that I want more gifts. What I want is the good that comes back to you from your giving, growing like savings in an account.

decisions.choice: not that I am angling for another gift
decisions.reason: A second disclaimer, like the one in verse 11: Paul's thanks are not a request for more.

decisions.choice: fruit: here, the return on an investment
alternatives: good character, the fruit of the Spirit
decisions.reason: In a passage full of business words, καρπός is the yield an investment produces. The gain is the Philippians', not Paul's.

decisions.choice: growing in your account
decisions.reason: λόγος is an account again, as in verse 15, and πλεονάζω means to increase. Their giving is like a deposit that keeps earning. The one who credits it is God, who will repay them (verse 19; compare Proverbs 19:17).

decisions.choice: profit that keeps adding up (B); growing like savings (R)
decisions.reason: "Fruit" on its own would suggest character, as in Galatians 5:22. Balanced and Readable keep the business picture; Literal keeps "fruit".

records.source: ἀπέχω δὲ πάντα καὶ περισσεύω· πεπλήρωμαι δεξάμενος παρὰ Ἐπαφροδίτου τὰ παρ’ ὑμῶν, ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας, θυσίαν δεκτήν, εὐάρεστον τῷ θεῷ.
records.gloss: I have received in full and all things and I abound; I have been filled having received from Epaphroditus the things from you, an aroma of fragrance, a sacrifice acceptable, well-pleasing to God.
pieces: Everything has been paid to me in full, and I have more than enough. Since Epaphroditus brought me what you sent, I have all I need. Your gift is a sweet-smelling offering, a sacrifice God accepts, one that pleases {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.18: But I have received all things in full, and I abound; I have been filled, having received from Epaphroditus the things from you, an aroma of fragrance, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God.

R.18: Think of this as my receipt: I have received everything in full, and more! Epaphroditus brought me your gifts, and now I have plenty. Your gifts are like a sacrifice offered to God, with a sweet smell. God gladly accepts them, and they please {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: I have received in full: the wording of a receipt
decisions.reason: ἀπέχω was the usual word on business receipts of the time, found in many papyrus documents: "received in full". Paul closes the account of verses 15-17 with a receipt, half in jest.

decisions.choice: I am filled: fully supplied
decisions.reason: πληρόω is the same verb as "will fill" in verse 19. The Philippians have filled Paul's need; God will fill theirs.

decisions.choice: the language of the offerings in the Law
decisions.reason: "An aroma of fragrance" is the phrase the Greek Old Testament uses for offerings that please God (Genesis 8:21; Leviticus 1:9). Paul treats their gift to him as a gift offered to God, as Ephesians 5:2 says of Christ's giving of himself.

decisions.choice: Epaphroditus, the church's messenger
decisions.reason: Epaphroditus brought the gift from Philippi and nearly died while serving Paul (2:25-30).

decisions.choice: paid to me in full
decisions.reason: Keeps the receipt language of the Greek.

decisions.choice: Think of this as my receipt
decisions.reason: Readers today would miss the receipt wording; Readable says what Paul is doing.

records.source: ὁ δὲ θεός μου πληρώσει πᾶσαν χρείαν ὑμῶν κατὰ τὸ πλοῦτος αὐτοῦ ἐν δόξῃ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
records.gloss: And the God of me will fill every need of you according to the riches of him in glory in Christ Jesus.
pieces: And my God will fill every need you have, in keeping with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} glorious wealth in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus.

L.19: And my God will fill every need of yours according to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} riches in glory in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus.

R.19: And my God will give you everything you need. God's riches are glorious and great, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} gives from them through {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus.

decisions.choice: my God, in turn, will fill your need
decisions.reason: Paul cannot repay them himself, but the God he serves will. "Will fill" is the same verb as "I am filled" in verse 18: they filled Paul's need, and God will fill theirs.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "will fill", a promise
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts have a form of the verb that turns the promise into a wish. The SBLGNT, with most manuscripts, has the future: a promise.

decisions.choice: glorious riches: "in glory" describes God's wealth
alternatives: he will fill your needs in a glorious way
decisions.reason: The Greek allows "in glory" to go with "his riches" or with "will fill". We read it with "riches", which it follows directly: the wealth from which God gives is his own, as glorious as he is. The other reading says the giving itself will be glorious. The difference is small, but a footnote gives it.

decisions.choice: in keeping with his wealth, not merely out of it
decisions.reason: κατά means "in proportion to": God gives on the scale of what he has, not a token from a great store.

decisions.choice: every need
decisions.reason: χρεία is the same word used of Paul's needs in verse 16. It is a promise about what they need, given to people who had just given generously.

decisions.choice: in Christ Jesus: God gives through his people's union with Christ
decisions.reason: The phrase ends the sentence and covers the whole promise: God's supply comes to them in and through Christ Jesus.

decisions.choice: glorious wealth (B); riches are glorious (R)
decisions.reason: "Riches in glory" is often heard as "riches in heaven". The adjective keeps the key term and follows meaning decision m3; Literal keeps "in glory".

decisions.choice: through
decisions.reason: Readable says how God's giving reaches them (meaning decision m6).

records.source: τῷ δὲ θεῷ καὶ πατρὶ ἡμῶν ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων· ἀμήν.
records.gloss: To the now God and Father of us the glory to the ages of the ages; amen.
pieces: Glory be to our God and Father for ever and ever. Amen.

L.20: Now to our God and Father [be] the glory to the ages of the ages. Amen.

R.20: Let all glory be given to our God and Father forever and ever. Amen.

decisions.choice: glory be given: an act of praise
decisions.reason: The Greek has no verb. Paul's other outbursts of praise (Romans 11:36; Galatians 1:5) are likewise praise offered, not information. "The glory" has the article: the glory that rightly belongs to God.

decisions.choice: God, who is our Father
alternatives: God, and our Father, as two persons
decisions.reason: One article covers both nouns, so they name the same person, as in 1:2.

decisions.choice: for ever and ever
alternatives: to the ages of the ages
decisions.reason: Literally "to the ages of the ages": a way of saying without end.

decisions.choice: Amen: "it is true, let it be so"
decisions.reason: ἀμήν is a Hebrew word carried over into Greek untranslated. Hearers said it to join in what was said.

decisions.choice: Amen
decisions.reason: Kept untranslated, as the Greek itself kept it; the word is familiar from prayer.

records.source: Ἀσπάσασθε πάντα ἅγιον ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
records.gloss: Greet every holy one in Christ Jesus.
pieces: Greet every one of God's holy people in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus.

L.21: Greet every holy one in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus.

R.21: Give my greetings to every one of God's people who belongs to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus.

decisions.choice: a holy one: a believer set apart as God's own
alternatives: a saint, a specially holy person
decisions.reason: ἅγιος describes every believer, not a select few; Paul greets the whole church this way in 1:1. Their holiness comes from God's claim on them, not from their own achievement.

decisions.choice: every single one
decisions.reason: The Greek is singular, "every holy one": each believer is greeted, with no one left out.

decisions.choice: holy in Christ Jesus
alternatives: greet them in Christ Jesus, as a fellow believer
decisions.reason: The phrase could go with "greet" or with "holy one". The same words describe the believers in 1:1, "the holy ones in Christ Jesus", so we read it with "holy one".

decisions.choice: holy one (L); God's holy people (B); God's people (R)
decisions.reason: "Saint" now usually means an exceptionally holy person, often one honored by a church after death. Paul means every believer.

decisions.choice: Give my greetings to
decisions.reason: The greeting comes from Paul through the church; Readable makes the sense of the command plain.

records.heading: Final greetings

records.source: ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς οἱ σὺν ἐμοὶ ἀδελφοί.
records.gloss: Greet you the with me brothers.
pieces: The {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} who are with me send you greetings.

L.21: The {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} with me greet you.

R.21: The {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} who are here with me send you their greetings.

decisions.choice: fellow believers with Paul, probably his co-workers
alternatives: all the believers where Paul is
decisions.reason: Verse 22 greets from "all the holy ones", so "the brothers with me" is probably the smaller circle working with Paul, such as Timothy (2:19-22). The word includes women when it means fellow believers, and Paul's co-workers included women (4:2-3). Whether women were in this group is not known.

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: No specific men are named and the word is the one used for fellow believers, so the inclusive default applies. Traditional is one tap away.

records.source: ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς πάντες οἱ ἅγιοι, μάλιστα δὲ οἱ ἐκ τῆς Καίσαρος οἰκίας.
records.gloss: Greet you all the holy ones, especially and those from the Caesar's household.
pieces: All God's holy people here greet you, especially those in the emperor's household.

L.22: All the holy ones greet you, but especially those of Caesar's household.

R.22: All of God's people here send you greetings, especially the believers who serve in the emperor's household.

decisions.choice: the emperor's staff: slaves and freed slaves in the imperial service
decisions.reason: "Caesar's household" was the large body of slaves and former slaves who ran the emperor's affairs, in Rome and in the provinces; many of them are named in inscriptions. It does not mean his relatives. That believers were among them shows the gospel had reached the heart of Roman government, as Paul hints in 1:13.

decisions.choice: Paul writes from a place where imperial servants are believers, most likely Rome
alternatives: Ephesus or Caesarea, where imperial servants also worked
decisions.reason: The letter does not name the place. Members of the imperial household served in Rome and in provincial centers, so this greeting does not settle the question on its own; with the palace guard in 1:13 it fits Rome best.

decisions.choice: holy ones: believers
decisions.reason: As in verse 21: all believers, set apart as God's own.

decisions.choice: the emperor's household
decisions.reason: By Paul's day "Caesar" was the emperor's title, not only a name; Literal keeps "Caesar".

decisions.choice: here
decisions.reason: The holy ones who greet them are the believers where Paul is; "here" makes that clear.

records.source: ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ὑμῶν.
records.gloss: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ with the spirit of you.
pieces: May the grace of the Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} be with your spirit.

L.23: The grace of the Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} [be] with your spirit.

R.23: May the grace of the Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} be with you, deep in your spirit.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "with your spirit"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read "with you all", the ending of some other letters (2 Thessalonians 3:18). Many manuscripts also add "Amen". The SBLGNT reading matches the endings of Galatians 6:18 and Philemon 25. The meaning is much the same.

decisions.choice: your spirit: you at the deepest level
decisions.reason: πνεῦμα is singular with a plural "your": the inner life of each of them, and perhaps their shared life as one church (1:27, "one spirit"). It does not refer to the Holy Spirit here.

decisions.choice: a prayer: may grace be with you
alternatives: a statement: grace is with you
decisions.reason: There is no verb. As with closing greetings generally, it is a blessing prayed over the readers.

decisions.choice: the letter ends where it began, with grace
decisions.reason: Paul opened with grace and peace (1:2) and closes with grace, the undeserved kindness of the Lord Jesus.

decisions.choice: with you, deep in your spirit
decisions.reason: "With your spirit" can sound odd in plain speech; Readable says the grace is with them, at the deepest level, and keeps the word "spirit".
